newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin wants more Western compromise on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin wants more Western compromise on NATO.

text.p: The Kremlin said on Wednesday that Russia was not prepared to sign a document defining post-Cold War relations with NATO later this month without further compromise from the West.

President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a news briefing that Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, who have held intensive talks in Luxembourg, had made some progress.
But Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin, who wants to sign the document in Paris on May 27, would not do so at any cost.
"Much more effort is needed from NATO as a bloc and from its members to reach mutually acceptable formulae which would allow us to sign the document," Yastrzhembsky said.

"Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) may go to Paris and take part in the signing if the final version of the text suits both NATO and Russia. If it does, then he will go and sign. If not, we are not limited by any time frames. We will keep on working."
Yastrzhembsky said that fresh talks between Primakov and Solana to minimise Russia's objections to NATO expansion would be held in Moscow next week.
These talks could help pave the way for Yeltsin to attend a NATO summit in Madrid in July at which the Western defence alliance will open the door to some ex-Warsaw Pact members.

Moscow, still stung by its post-communist loss of superpower status, had previously ruled out Yeltsin's participation in the Madrid summit where Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to receive invitations to join the alliance.
But Deputy Russian Foreign Minister Igor Ivanov said that Yeltsin had told visiting Spanish King Juan Carlos, who said he would be glad to welcome the Kremlin leader in Madrid, that he might go.
"President Yeltsin replied that the issue would be considered, taking into account all factors," Ivanov told reporters without elaborating.

Moscow says nothing will make it drop its objections to the expansion, but it wants to minimise what it sees as a threat to its own and European security by signing a document defining Russian-NATO relations into the 21st century.
Echoing a new conciliatory line coming from Moscow, Ivanov said that at talks both sides agreed that they should minimise the negative consequences of the expansion.
Yeltsin, in an interview with the Krasnaya Zvezda newspaper published on Wednesday, appeared to be preparing Russian public opinion for a compromise on the NATO issue.
"We will do everything to minimise the consequences for Russia's security of a possible expansion of NATO," he said, emphasising efforts to integrate with former Soviet republics.
But Yeltsin still faces continued strong opposition from communists and nationalists, who said they would picket in front of NATO-country embassies in Moscow on Thursday.

Russia has been demanding strict curbs on any military activities in any new NATO member states, but the Western alliance says such demands are out of the question because such issues are a matter of national sovereignty.
"As you understand this topic is very delicate. Negotiations are very difficult," Ivanov said.
